messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Weber is a 49-year-old married fashion designer who came to treatment after months of telling himself he just needed to stay busy. The event he returns to, against his will and in fragments, is not something that happened to him directly but to his wife. About a year ago, she was seriously injured in a violent accident while the two of them were out together after one of his industry events. He remembers the evening first through isolated, piercing images rather than as a continuous sequence: the look on her face a split second before impact, the sound of her hitting the ground, the unnatural stillness afterward, his own hands shaking as he tried to reach her. Other stretches are simply absent. When he tries to tell the story, he can describe one second with unbearable precision and then finds there is nothing where the next several minutes should be. That unevenness troubles him. He has come to believe there are things he should remember and that if he cannot, it says something damning about him.

What comes back most forcefully is guilt. When the memory surfaces, Martin does not merely feel sad or frightened; he is hit by a wave of shame and self-reproach so intense that he has to break off whatever he is doing. He becomes certain, in those moments, that he failed her in some fundamental way. He revisits tiny decisions from that evening—where they stood, when they left, what he noticed and did not notice—and experiences them as accusations. If he starts to picture her on the pavement, he feels his chest tighten, his stomach drop, and his skin prickle. Sometimes his heart pounds so hard he has to brace himself against a table or sit down until it passes. He describes these episodes as his body reacting before he has fully understood what has set him off.

Since the accident, Martin has tried to manage by narrowing his life. At work, he used to enjoy the forward motion of fashion seasons—sketching collections months ahead, discussing future campaigns, booking travel, talking excitedly about what came next. Now he avoids making plans whenever he can. When his team asks about next season’s concepts or deadlines beyond the immediate week, he deflects, tells them they will decide later, or pushes decisions onto others. The idea of picturing the future feels wrong to him, as if doing so is unsafe or presumptuous. His world has contracted to whatever must be handled today.

He also works hard not to think about the accident at all. He keeps music or podcasts on constantly in the studio, answers emails late into the night, reorganizes fabric libraries, redraws pieces that do not need redrawing. The busyness is deliberate. If his mind is occupied every second, he thinks, maybe the images will not break through. At home he does the same, scrolling, cleaning, turning on the television without really watching it. His wife has noticed that he rarely sits still with her anymore. What was once a shared evening on the couch has become Martin pacing the apartment with his phone in his hand, searching for anything that will keep his mind from settling.

The suppression does not spare him at night. Sleep has become erratic and strained. He lies awake dreading the quiet because the quiet makes room for memory. On other nights he falls asleep from exhaustion only to wake again, already tense, his body flooded as though the event were present in the room. By morning he is depleted and irritable, carrying a heavy mix of fear, anger, and guilt he finds difficult to explain. He is ashamed of how emotionally raw he has become, particularly because he sees himself as the one who should be steady.

The reminders that catch him are often ordinary and therefore hard to control. In his work, fittings and runway preparations involve sudden noise, crowded movement, and the sight of someone stumbling in high heels or being hurried through a space. A model losing balance backstage can make his whole body jolt before he can think. Even seeing his wife pause awkwardly or wince from lingering effects of her injuries can send him into a rush of dread and self-blame. He tries to hide these reactions, stepping away under the pretense of taking a call or checking on a garment rack, but his assistants have begun to notice that he disappears at tense moments and no longer seems fully present.

By the time he sought help, Martin was exhausted by the effort of containing all of this. He and his wife had started arguing about his distance, especially his refusal to talk about anything beyond the next few days. He knew his work was changing too; colleagues experienced him as evasive and indecisive, and he privately feared he was losing the part of himself that could imagine and create. What finally brought him in was the realization that even with constant distraction, the memory still forced its way through and left him overwhelmed. He said he wants to be able to remember what happened without feeling crushed by guilt and without his body reacting as if it is happening again. What frightens him most is the possibility that if he stops holding everything at bay, he will be overtaken completely.
